topics.title: 10.1 Blocks
topics.summary: A block is a unit of storage managed by the allocator. It may contain a header, a payload returned to the caller, and padding. The caller’s requested size and the allocator’s actual block size can differ. A 13-byte request might occupy a larger block because of alignment or size classes. The fundamental invariant is that live allocation payloads do not overlap and remain valid until release. A custom allocator should state its supported alignments, maximum request size, zero-size policy, and threading model. Without those declarations, callers cannot know whether a returned address is appropriate for their object.

topics.title: 10.2 Metadata
topics.summary: Metadata records information such as block size, allocation state, neighboring blocks, or free-list links. It can be stored next to the payload or in separate tables. Adjacent metadata is convenient but can be corrupted by an out-of-bounds write from the payload. Never treat allocator metadata as trustworthy after detecting memory corruption. Continuing to allocate and free through damaged state can amplify the failure. A teaching allocator can use assertions and validation scans; a production allocator also needs careful hardening, concurrency control, and recovery policy. Implementing an allocator is not just writing a fast search loop.

topics.title: 10.3 Free lists
topics.summary: A free list links blocks available for reuse. An implicit list discovers free blocks by walking every block’s metadata. An explicit list links free blocks directly, often storing links inside the free payload. Segregated lists group blocks by size to reduce search cost. Every insertion and removal must preserve list consistency. A block must not appear twice, and an allocated block must not remain on a free list. In a concurrent allocator, these are shared-state invariants requiring synchronization or a carefully proved lock-free scheme. Thread-local caches reduce contention but can retain memory that another thread could otherwise use.

topics.title: 10.4 First fit
topics.summary: First fit scans candidates and selects the first block large enough. It is simple and can stop early, but its behavior depends on list order. Over time, small leftover regions near the beginning can increase search work or change fragmentation patterns. A first-fit policy is not inherently bad; its suitability depends on request sizes, lifetimes, and workload locality. Measure representative traces rather than judging a policy by one allocation. Search cost, fragmentation, cache behavior, and synchronization overhead can move in different directions.

topics.title: 10.5 Best fit
topics.summary: Best fit selects the smallest available block that can satisfy the request. It tries to minimize the immediate leftover amount, but finding that block can require more search or a more complex index. Small leftovers can also become unusable fragments. The name describes a local choice, not a proof of globally optimal memory use. Future requests are unknown. A slightly larger current remainder might be more useful later than a tiny one. Compare allocator policies using complete traces and explicit metrics rather than assuming that the word “best” guarantees the best outcome.

topics.title: 10.7 Coalescing
topics.summary: Coalescing merges adjacent free blocks into a larger free region. It reduces external fragmentation by restoring space that can satisfy larger requests. Adjacency means neighboring addresses in the managed region, not neighboring nodes in an arbitrary free-list order. Boundary tags or external metadata can help find physical neighbors. Immediate coalescing merges on each release; deferred coalescing postpones work until needed. Either policy must avoid merging across live blocks or unrelated regions. A correct merge removes old list entries before inserting the combined block exactly once.

topics.title: 10.8 Alignment
topics.summary: The allocator must align the payload, not merely the block header. A header whose size is not a multiple of the requested alignment can misalign the returned address. The allocator may add padding before the payload and must retain enough information to find the actual block on release. For an arena, alignment consumes part of the remaining space before the requested bytes are reserved. Check both components. C++ std::align can help find an aligned subregion within a bounded span of storage. It does not allocate more memory or initialize an object; it only adjusts a pointer and available-space description.

topics.title: 10.9 Internal fragmentation
topics.summary: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block, such as rounding a 13-byte request to a 16-byte size class. The application owns the block’s payload contract but may not be allowed to use all allocator-internal spare bytes. Measure internal fragmentation as actual reserved bytes minus requested useful bytes under a clearly stated accounting rule. Headers and alignment padding may be reported separately or included; consistency matters. A small per-object waste becomes substantial when millions of objects are live.

topics.title: 10.10 External fragmentation
topics.summary: External fragmentation occurs when free space is divided into regions that cannot satisfy a larger request even though their total size is sufficient. Two free 40-byte regions separated by a live block cannot satisfy one contiguous 64-byte request. Coalescing helps only when free regions are physically adjacent. Compaction could move live objects, but ordinary raw pointers make transparent movement difficult. Handles, indirection, or moving-memory runtimes can support compaction; a conventional C allocator cannot simply relocate an arbitrary live allocation without the program’s cooperation.

topics.title: 10.11 Arena allocation
topics.summary: An arena obtains a region and serves allocations from it, often by advancing a cursor. Individual deallocation may be omitted; all storage is reset together. This makes allocation fast and cleanup simple when objects share a lifetime, such as one parsed document or request. Resetting an arena invalidates every object and view backed by it. Nontrivial C++ objects may need destructors before reset, and retained pointers must not escape the arena’s lifetime. An arena trades flexible reclamation for a stronger lifetime discipline. It is excellent when that discipline matches the problem and dangerous when callers assume independent object lifetimes.

topics.summary: Imagine three consecutive heap blocks: allocated 64, free 80, free 48. Coalescing reduces external fragmentation because future large requests can use space that was previously split into smaller holes.

topics.title: Staged project — A reusable free-list allocator
topics.summary: The bump arena is intentionally retained because it isolates alignment and bounded allocation. The next implementation adds individual deallocation and combines the mechanisms introduced in Sections 10.1 through 10.10. Its contract is deliberately narrower than malloc : it manages one fixed 512-byte region, returns storage aligned to 16 bytes, accepts only pointers returned by its own allocate , uses first fit, splits only when the remainder is at least 32 bytes, and immediately coalesces physically adjacent free blocks. It is single-threaded and does not construct C++ objects. Companion listing: ch10/freelist_allocator.cpp The companion listing contains the complete definitions and executable tests. Keeping block descriptors in a vector rather than inside the managed bytes makes the teaching invariant easier to inspect: descriptors are in increasing address order, their half-open ranges exactly partition [0, 512) , and no two live allocations overlap. A production allocator would normally avoid allocating metadata dynamically while servicing an allocation request. Allocation trace. Begin with [0,512) F . Allocate 64 bytes: [0,64) A [64,512) F . Allocate 80 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,512) F . Allocate 48 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,192) A [192,512) F . Free the middle block: [0,64) A [64,144) F [144,192) A [192,512) F . A 32-byte request reuses the 80-byte hole and splits it because the 48-byte remainder exceeds the minimum split: [0,64) A [64,96) A [96,144) F [144,192) A [192,512) F . Coalescing trace. Free [0,64) , then [64,96) . The allocator first merges left with the newly free block and then merges the adjacent [96,144) remainder, producing [0,144) F . Freeing [144,192) merges on both sides as applicable; the final free of the last live block restores [0,512) F . The test therefore exercises reuse, left coalescing, right coalescing, and restoration of the original region. Statistics distinguish requested bytes from reserved bytes. Their difference is internal fragmentation under this implementation’s rounding rule. External fragmentation can be reported as free_bytes - largest_free : zero means every free byte is currently in one contiguous block. These metrics are policy-dependent descriptions, not universal allocator-quality scores. The implementation rejects zero-sized requests, arithmetic that would overflow during alignment rounding, pointers outside the arena, pointers into the interior of a block, and a second release of a block that is still represented as free. These checks are intentionally limited. After coalescing, stale pointers can coincide with a later allocation start, corrupted metadata can invalidate the reasoning, and address reuse makes perfect temporal error detection impossible without additional generation or quarantine metadata. Sanitizers and hardened allocators use stronger mechanisms; this example does not claim complete invalid-free detection. Allocator project tests. Verify exhaustion without state corruption; reuse of a freed first-fit block; 16-byte alignment for every successful result; refusal to create a remainder smaller than 32 bytes; coalescing with a free predecessor, successor, and both neighbors; invalid and double-free rejection for the cases above; overflow-checked size rounding; and conservation of the 512 managed bytes after every operation.

An allocator converts larger regions of storage into smaller allocations while tracking which regions are available. SLIDE 22: 10.10 External fragmentation

LECTURE NARRATION
External fragmentation occurs when free space is divided into regions that cannot satisfy a larger request even though their total size is sufficient. Two free 40-byte regions separated by a live block cannot satisfy one contiguous 64-byte request. Coalescing helps only when free regions are physically adjacent. Compaction could move live objects, but ordinary raw pointers make transparent movement difficult. Handles, indirection, or moving-memory runtimes can support compaction; a conventional C allocator cannot simply relocate an arbitrary live allocation without the program’s cooperation.

SLIDE 24: 10.11 Arena allocation

LECTURE NARRATION
An arena obtains a region and serves allocations from it, often by advancing a cursor. Individual deallocation may be omitted; all storage is reset together. This makes allocation fast and cleanup simple when objects share a lifetime, such as one parsed document or request. Resetting an arena invalidates every object and view backed by it. Nontrivial C++ objects may need destructors before reset, and retained pointers must not escape the arena’s lifetime. An arena trades flexible reclamation for a stronger lifetime discipline. It is excellent when that discipline matches the problem and dangerous when callers assume independent object lifetimes.

SLIDE 32: Staged project — A reusable free-list allocator

LECTURE NARRATION
The bump arena is intentionally retained because it isolates alignment and bounded allocation. The next implementation adds individual deallocation and combines the mechanisms introduced in Sections 10.1 through 10.10. Its contract is deliberately narrower than malloc : it manages one fixed 512-byte region, returns storage aligned to 16 bytes, accepts only pointers returned by its own allocate , uses first fit, splits only when the remainder is at least 32 bytes, and immediately coalesces physically adjacent free blocks. It is single-threaded and does not construct C++ objects. Companion listing: ch10/freelist_allocator.cpp The companion listing contains the complete definitions and executable tests. Keeping block descriptors in a vector rather than inside the managed bytes makes the teaching invariant easier to inspect: descriptors are in increasing address order, their half-open ranges exactly partition [0, 512) , and no two live allocations overlap. A production allocator would normally avoid allocating metadata dynamically while servicing an allocation request. Allocation trace. Begin with [0,512) F . Allocate 64 bytes: [0,64) A [64,512) F . Allocate 80 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,512) F . Allocate 48 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,192) A [192,512) F . Free the middle block: [0,64) A [64,144) F [144,192) A [192,512) F . Free [0,64) , then [64,96) . The allocator first merges left with the newly free block and then merges the adjacent [96,144) remainder, producing [0,144) F . Freeing [144,192) merges on both sides as applicable; the final free of the last live block restores [0,512) F . The test therefore exercises reuse, left coalescing, right coalescing, and restoration of the original region. Statistics distinguish requested bytes from reserved bytes. Their difference is internal fragmentation under this implementation’s rounding rule. External fragmentation can be reported as free_bytes - largest_free : zero means every free byte is currently in one contiguous block. These metrics are policy-dependent descriptions, not universal allocator-quality scores. The implementation rejects zero-sized requests, arithmetic that would overflow during alignment rounding, pointers outside the arena, pointers into the interior of a block, and a second release of a block that is still represented as free. These checks are intentionally limited. After coalescing, stale pointers can coincide with a later allocation start, corrupted metadata can invalidate the reasoning, and address reuse makes perfect temporal error detection impossible without additional generation or quarantine metadata. Sanitizers and hardened allocators use stronger mechanisms; this example does not claim complete invalid-free detection. Allocator project tests.
